entry.content:

An update to the Chromium Flatpak runtime that upgraded glibc from version 2.31 to 2.33 accidentally broke audio and video playback by triggering fatal crashes in Chromium's audio service. Debugging revealed that glibc encountered unexpected error codes from the futex facility, causing it to abort execution.

Further investigation traced the issue to a glibc commit that modified condition variable handling to always pass a clock identifier, resulting in the inclusion of the FUTEX_CLOCK_REALTIME flag even when no timeout was specified. Chromium's strict BPF audio service sandbox rejected this unexpected flag because it was missing from the allowed syscall rules, ultimately terminating the audio process.

entry.title: Goose Memory-Safe Systems Programming Language Introduced
entry.content:
Links: aardappel.github.io | hacker news

Goose is a memory-safe systems programming language designed without a heap allocator, garbage collector, reference counting, or lifetime annotations. Utilizing syntax familiar to C and Rust programmers, the language relies on compiler-managed data stacks where memory growth advances a pointer and scope exit automatically frees resources. Benchmarks provided by the project indicate that Goose achieves faster execution and lower memory consumption compared to idiomatic C++ and safe Rust.

The language enforces safety through static lifetime inference without requiring explicit lifetime syntax or aliasing rules, while its underlying memory model ensures that references remain valid during array expansion. Additional architectural features include variable-mode algebraic data types, position-independent relative references that double as file formats without serialization, and guaranteed in-place construction. Goose compiles directly to a single C file and supports execution via a bundled TinyCC backend.

entry.title: Incremental Computation Graphs Overview
entry.content:
Links: dziban.net | discussion

Incremental computation graphs use mutable inputs and pure, memoized functions to track dependencies and minimize redundant execution during development tasks like code compilation and type-checking. Developed as part of the Yabu programming language project and inspired by Salsa, the system builds a runtime dependency graph where computations are dynamically linked to their source inputs.

When an input changes, a red-green walk algorithm checks revision timestamps along the dependency chain, invalidating only the affected computations while returning cached results for everything else. This selective invalidation allows compilers and typecheckers to operate at interactive speeds even across large codebases.

entry.title: Analysis of Undefined Behavior Consequences and Compiler Optimizations in C and C++
entry.content:
Links: blog.habets.se | discussion

A technical blog post examines misconceptions surrounding undefined behavior (UB) in C and C++ programming, demonstrating how modern compilers like GCC and Clang handle faulty code during optimization. Using concrete examples involving `std::unreachable()` and null pointer dereferences, the analysis shows that UB can result in unpredictable execution paths, such as uncalled functions running or unexpected memory modifications rather than a simple segmentation fault.

Because compilers treat undefined behavior as an impossibility rather than an error condition, optimization passes can drastically alter program logic in counterintuitive ways. The assembly output examples illustrate that developers cannot rely on intuition or legacy assumptions about how runtime environments handle erroneous code, underscoring why UB remains a persistent hazard in systems programming.
